planting.note: Direct sow in spring in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; composite dropseed tolerates dry, rocky, or sandy soils across a wide native range from the Great Plains to the East Coast and is very slow to establish from seed like its relative prairie dropseed, so plugs or divisions are often preferred for a faster start.

directions: Composite dropseed forms a coarser, more upright clump than prairie dropseed, with narrow arching leaves topped by tall, wiry flowering culms that hold slender, partially enclosed seed heads well above the foliage from late summer into fall. It thrives in the same lean, infertile, well-drained soils that punish richer garden plants, and needs no supplemental fertilizer or irrigation once its deep root system is established. Use it in dry prairie restorations, meadow plantings, or as a tough textural accent along a sunny border edge, leaving the seed heads standing through winter for finches and sparrows. Cut the clump back to a few inches in early spring before new growth resumes.

planting.note: Direct sow or set out divisions in spring in lean, rocky, well-drained soil in full sun; mountain muhly is native to dry, rocky slopes and open coniferous woodlands at mid-to-high elevation across the Southern Rockies and Southwest, and is adapted to cool nights and short growing seasons.

directions: Mountain muhly forms a fine-textured, silvery-green tufted bunchgrass well suited to xeriscape and high-elevation rock garden plantings, producing slender purplish-tinged seed heads in late summer that age to a soft tan through fall. It is exceptionally drought and cold tolerant once established, thriving in lean, rocky, or gravelly soils where richer plants struggle, and needs no supplemental irrigation beyond an establishment period. Use it as a fine-textured accent among boulders, in a xeric border, or interplanted with penstemon and other high-desert perennials. Trim old foliage back in early spring before new growth begins.

planting.note: Direct sow or plant divisions in spring in moist to seasonally wet, alkaline or saline soil in full sun; scratchgrass is native to alkaline meadows, seeps, and disturbed moist ground across much of North America and is notably tolerant of salty and alkaline conditions that exclude most other grasses.

directions: Scratchgrass is a low, fine-textured, rhizomatous grass that spreads by slender underground stems to form an open mat, producing delicate, airy purplish-green seed panicles in late summer. Its standout trait is tolerance of alkaline and saline soils and seasonally wet, poorly drained ground where few other ornamental grasses persist, making it a useful groundcover for disturbed alkaline flats, roadside swales, or the edges of irrigation ditches and stock ponds. It spreads readily in favorable moist conditions, so give it room or a contained bed where an assertive spreading habit is welcome rather than a problem. Mow or cut back old growth in early spring before new shoots emerge.

planting.note: Direct sow or plant divisions in spring in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; Cimarron was released for its strong performance and heat tolerance in the southern Great Plains and adapts well to hot, dry summers.

directions: Cimarron little bluestem is an Oklahoma-origin selection of the classic native prairie grass, chosen for reliable establishment and vigor under the hot, dry summers typical of the southern Plains. It forms the same upright, blue-green clumping habit as the species, turning warm copper-orange in fall with fluffy silver seed tufts that persist into winter for bird interest and garden texture. Plant it in lean, well-drained soil in full sun, where it will outperform richer-soil plantings and require no supplemental fertilizer once established. Cut the clump back to a few inches in late winter before new growth resumes.

planting.note: Direct sow or plant divisions in spring in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; Camper is a Nebraska-origin release valued for its leafiness and adaptation to the cooler, drier conditions of the central and western Great Plains.

directions: Camper little bluestem is a Nebraska-developed selection noted for its dense, leafy basal growth and good winter hardiness across the cooler northern and central Plains. Like the species, it forms an upright, fine-textured clump of blue-green summer foliage that shifts to rich russet and copper tones in fall, with silvery seed tufts held on wiry stems into winter. It is highly drought tolerant once established and performs best in lean, well-drained soil in full sun, without added fertilizer. Cut back to a few inches in late winter before new growth begins to keep the clump tidy.
